title: 2D arrays and matrices
overview: Module 14 moves from rows of values to grids. A 2D array `a[n][m]` is an array of rows, and each element is reached with two indexes: `a[i][j]`. With nested loops you can read, change and print a matrix, and test for special shapes such as scalar matrices or diagonals. The practice files also bring back the frequency-array trick.

concepts.explain: `int a[3][4]` is 3 rows, each holding 4 ints, for 12 cells in total. `a[i][j]` is row `i`, column `j`, and both start at 0.
The outer loop picks the row `i` and the inner loop walks the columns `j`. For output, print a newline after each row.
In memory the rows sit one after another. That is why `scanf` fills the grid the same way whether the input has 12 numbers on one line or 4 numbers on each of 3 lines.
The cells where `i == j`, running from top-left to bottom-right. Only a square matrix has diagonals.
The cells where `i + j == n - 1`, running from top-right to bottom-left.
A diagonal matrix has zeros everywhere off the diagonal. A scalar matrix also has the same value everywhere on the diagonal. A unit matrix is a scalar matrix with 1s on the diagonal.
Start with `flag = 1`, meaning "yes so far". Set it to 0 on the first cell that breaks the rule, then print based on `flag`.

files.title: 2D array addresses: the rows are one strip of memory
files.what: Prints every cell of a 3×5 array with its row, column, memory address and value. The point is the address column: it goes up by 4 every cell and keeps going up by 4 when a new row starts, which is what "a 2D array is stored row after row" actually means. (This file used to be saved as `basic.py` by mistake — it was always C, so it is `basic.c` now.)
steps: `int arr[3][5]` is filled with a brace list, one inner list per row: 1 to 5, then 6 to 10, then 11 to 15.
The outer loop `i` goes over the 3 rows, and the inner loop `j` goes over the 5 columns, so the cells come out in memory order.
For each cell it prints `i`, `j`, the address `&arr[i][j]` with `%p`, and the value `arr[i][j]` with `%d`.
`&arr[i][j]` is cast to `(void*)` because that is the type `%p` expects.
A newline after each inner loop puts one row of the array on one line of the screen.
files.output_note: Fifteen cells, five to a line. Read the address column down the page: `...FDE0`, `...FDE4`, `...FDE8` — 4 bytes apart, the size of one `int`. Now look at the jump from the end of row 0 (`...FDF0`, value 5) to the start of row 1 (`...FDF4`, value 6): still 4. There is no gap between the rows. The 15 cells are one straight strip of 60 bytes, and the `[i][j]` pair is just a convenient way to name a place in it. The addresses themselves will differ on your machine; only the steps of 4 matter.
files.watch_out: The number of placeholders in the format string must match the number of values after it, in the same order. One `%d` too many and `printf` reads a value nobody passed — it prints rubbish, and gcc says nothing unless you compile with `-Wall`.

check.q: If `arr[0][4]` is at address 1000, where is `arr[1][0]`, and why?
check.a: 1004. Row 1 starts in the very next `int`, because the rows are stored one after another with nothing in between.

files.title: Read, change and print a matrix
files.what: Reads an n×m matrix, overwrites two cells, and prints the grid. It is the basic template for 2D input and output.
steps: Read `n` rows and `m` columns. Declare `a[n+5][m+5]` to leave a little spare room.
The nested loops read every `a[i][j]` in row order.
`a[1][2] = 100` and `a[2][3] = 200` change single cells, counting from 0.
The nested loops print each row, with a newline after it.
files.input_note: A 3×4 matrix, one row per line.
files.output_note: The same grid, except that 7 (row 1, column 2) is now `100` and 12 (row 2, column 3) is now `200`.
files.watch_out: The program writes to `a[2][3]` without checking the size. With n < 3 or m < 4 that cell isn't part of your data. The `+5` padding hides the problem instead of fixing it.

check.q: Which input value does `a[1][2]` replace in the sample?

files.title: Is the matrix scalar?
files.what: Checks that every diagonal cell equals `m[0][0]` and every other cell is 0.
steps: Read `n` and the n×n matrix `m`.
Save `element = m[0][0]` and set `flag = 1`.
Go through every cell. If `i == j`, the cell must equal `element`. Otherwise it must be 0.
On a failure, set `flag = 0` and `break`. This only leaves the inner loop.
Print `Scaler` or `Not Scaler` depending on `flag`.
files.input_note: A 3×3 matrix with 5s on the diagonal.
files.output_note: `Scaler`: every diagonal cell is 5 and every other cell is 0.
files.watch_out: `break` only leaves the inner loop, so the outer loop keeps going. The answer is still right, but it wastes time. You could also add `if(!flag) break;` to the outer loop.

check.a: No. It is diagonal, but the diagonal values (3, 3, 0) are not all equal.

files.title: Diagonal difference
files.what: Adds up each diagonal of a square matrix and prints the absolute difference between the two sums.
steps: Read `n` and the n×n matrix.
In one pass over the cells: if `i == j`, add the cell to `main_diagonal`. If `i + j == n - 1`, add it to `sec_diagonal`.
Both checks are plain `if`s, not `if / else if`, so the centre cell of an odd-sized matrix goes into both sums.
Print `abs(main_diagonal - sec_diagonal)`.
files.output_note: `1`: the main diagonal is 1+5+10 = 16, the secondary diagonal is 3+5+9 = 17, and |16−17| = 1.
files.watch_out: You don't need two loops. `for i: main += m[i][i]; sec += m[i][n-1-i];` does the same work in O(n).

check.q: In a 4×4 matrix, which column holds the secondary-diagonal cell of row 1?

files.title: Unique characters in sorted order
files.what: Prints each different lowercase letter of a word once, in alphabetical order, using a 26-slot presence array.
steps: Read the given length, then the word into `str`, which is sized `length + 1`.
For each lowercase character, set `freq[str[i] - 'a'] = 1`.
Loop over `i` from 0 to 25 and print `i + 'a'` wherever `freq[i]` is 1.
End with a newline.
files.input_note: The first line is the length the problem gives. Here it is 7, but `banana` has 6 letters. The code uses `strlen`, so a wrong length still works as long as it isn't too small.
files.output_note: `abn`: the letters a, b and n, in alphabetical order.
files.watch_out: If the given length is smaller than the real word, `str[length+1]` overflows. Size the buffer from the limits (for example 100005), not from the input.

check.q: What does the program print for `apple`?

files.title: Count distinct numbers
files.what: Counts how many different values the array has. Each value is counted the first time its slot is still 0.
steps: Read `n` and the array.
`freq[100001]` starts at zeros, and `unique_count` starts at 0.
For each `arr[i]`: if `freq[arr[i]]` is still 0, set it to 1 and add 1 to `unique_count`.
Print `unique_count`.
files.input_note: 7 numbers, and several of them repeat.
files.watch_out: `freq[100001]` covers values up to 100000, which matches the limit `A[i] <= 10^5`.

check.q: How many distinct values are there in `5 5 5 5`?

files.title: Count Letters (practice)
files.what: Prints how many times each lowercase letter appears in a string, in alphabetical order. It is the frequency array of Module 13 applied to letters.
steps: The string can hold 10^7 characters, so `s` is declared above `main`. A local array that big would not fit in the stack, and a global array also starts at zero.
`int freq[26] = {0};` keeps one box per letter: box 0 for `a`, box 25 for `z`.
`strlen` is called once, before the loop, because it walks the whole string every time it is called.
For each character, `s[i] - 'a'` gives its box number, and `freq[...]++` adds one to that box.
The last loop walks the boxes from 0 to 25 and prints `letter : count` for every box above zero.
files.input_note: The first sample from the statement.
files.output_note: Three lines, `a : 3`, `b : 2` and `c : 1`, which is what the statement expects.
files.watch_out: The letters come out sorted because the boxes are walked in order, not because anything was sorted. Only lowercase letters are safe here: an uppercase letter would give a box number above 25.

check.q: Why is `strlen` called once into `length` instead of being used in the loop condition?
check.a: `strlen` walks the string to find the `'\0'`. Inside the condition it would do that on every pass, turning one walk into 10^7 walks.

files.title: Search in matrix (practice)

problem.name: Codeforces group - S. Search in matrix

files.what: Reads a grid and a number `x`, then says whether `x` is somewhere in the grid. It is the array search of Module 7 with one loop more.
steps: Read `n` and `m`, then fill `a[n][m]` with two nested loops.
Read the number `x` that is being looked for.
`found` starts at 0 and becomes 1 the moment a cell equals `x`.
The inner `break` leaves the current row only, so a second `if(found == 1) break;` is needed to leave the outer loop as well.
Print `will not take number` when `found` is 1, otherwise `will take number`.
files.complexity: Time O(n × m) · Space O(n × m)
files.input_note: The sample from the statement: a 3 × 3 grid and the number 5.
files.output_note: `will not take number`, because 5 is in the grid (first row and second row).
files.watch_out: One `break` only leaves the loop it sits in. Without the second check the outer loop would keep walking the remaining rows.

check.q: Why is a single `found` flag enough, even when `x` appears more than once?
check.a: The question is only whether `x` is there at all, so the first match already decides the answer.

recap: `a[i][j]` means row `i`, column `j`, both starting at 0. Use nested loops to visit every cell.
Main diagonal: `i == j`. Secondary diagonal: `i + j == n - 1`.
A matrix is diagonal, scalar or unit depending on its off-diagonal zeros and diagonal values.
Use a flag to record "the rule broke somewhere".
Rows are stored one after another, so input line breaks don't matter to `scanf`.

check_yourself.q: How many cells does `int arr[3][3]` have?
Does a 4×3 matrix have a primary diagonal?
check_yourself.a: No. Diagonals are only defined for square matrices.

check_yourself.q: Is a unit matrix also a scalar matrix?
check_yourself.a: Yes. It is the scalar matrix whose diagonal value is 1.

body: A list of numbers is something you can already handle. `int a[5]` is a line of five boxes, and `a[2]` picks the third one. This module is about what happens when the numbers do not lie in a line but sit in a grid.
The everyday version is a marks sheet. Three students down the side, three subjects across the top, and one mark in every box:
intro.trace:
Bangla  English  Maths
student 0       7        8       9
student 1       4        5       6
student 2       1        2       3

body: With one index only, you can still store this, but it gets ugly. You could keep three separate arrays, `s0`, `s1` and `s2`, one per student. Then you cannot loop over the students at all, because a loop can change a number but not the name of a variable.

Or you could put all nine marks in one long array of nine boxes, and work out by hand that the mark of student `i` in subject `j` sits at position `3*i + j`. That works, but you redo that little sum every single time, and it changes the moment the number of subjects changes.
C gives you the grid directly. `int a[3][3]` is three rows, and each row is an array of three ints. You reach one box with two indexes: `a[i][j]` is row `i`, column `j`, and both start counting at 0.
intro.trace:
j=0  j=1  j=2
i=0      7    8    9
i=1      4    5    6
i=2      1    2    3

a[0][2] = 9   (row 0, column 2)
a[2][0] = 1   (row 2, column 0)
a[1][1] = 5   (the middle box)

body: That is the new thing here: until now an index was one number picking one box; now the first number picks the row and the second picks the box inside that row. Nothing else about arrays changes.
Two indexes means two loops, one inside the other. The outer loop holds a row still while the inner loop walks across it:
Read that again slowly. For one value of `i` the whole inner loop runs from start to finish, so the boxes are visited row by row:

Swap the two loops and the same nine boxes come out column by column instead. The `printf("\n")` belongs to the outer loop, because a row ends when the inner loop has finished; move it inside and every single number lands on its own line. Reading a grid is the same shape, with `scanf("%d", &a[i][j])` in place of the `printf`.

**A second example.** On a square grid the boxes where `i == j`, that is (0,0), (1,1) and (2,2), form the line from the top-left corner to the bottom-right one. That is the main diagonal, and one loop adding `a[i][i]` totals it. The other diagonal is the boxes where `i + j == n - 1`: in a 3×3 grid, (0,2), (1,1) and (2,0).

**A third example.** To answer "is every box off the diagonal a zero?" you need no new tool. Start with `flag = 1`, meaning "true so far", walk every box, and set `flag = 0` the moment one box breaks the rule. It is the same flag you have used with ordinary loops.

**Why bother.** A great many things are shaped like a grid: a chessboard, a picture made of pixels, a table of distances between cities, a class timetable. Writing `a[i][j]` with two loops is short enough that you can spend your thinking on the actual question instead of on where the numbers live.
The programs below read and print a matrix, test whether one is scalar, measure the gap between the two diagonals, and end with two problems that bring back the frequency array from Module 13.
